title: Latency-first shard orchestration and KV coalescing (brainstorm)
content:
Purpose:
This doc collects a set of rough ideas and micro-designs for a latency-first multi-GPU serving strategy that biases routing, KV cache placement, and collective choices to minimize tail-RTT for small-to-medium single-request workloads (the common hosted API case). Goal is to capture heuristics we can prototype quickly, list measurable experiments, and call out low-risk rollout paths.

Context and motivation:
- We observed in recent production traces that 65% of API calls are under 512 tokens and are latency-sensitive (p95 target < 120 ms for the 8k-token models).
- Current default sharding (symmetric tensor+KV spread) favors throughput and even memory use but incurs p95 penalty when model steps require cross-GPU collectives (alltoall/allreduce) under noisy NIC conditions.
- We want a fallback that optimizes for lower serialization + fewer collectives for single-request flows while preserving throughput for batchy workloads.

High-level idea (latency-first orchestration):
1) Split client requests into two classes at the ingress layer: latency-sensitive (single or small microbatch) vs throughput-oriented (large microbatches).
2) For latency-sensitive, prefer shard placements that reduce inter-GPU hops for KV lookups and attention kernels even if it slightly increases memory pressure (vertical affinity).
3) Coalesce KV cache reads into single-stage local prefetch where possible, and route requests to the GPU holding the primary hot-slice of KV for that prompt prefix.
4) Use NCCL tuning profile that favors p2p and ring collectives optimized for low-latency (lower rendezvous, smaller fragments) for these flows.
5) Provide dynamic fallback that switches to default balanced sharding when throughput is dominant or when memory limits are hit.

Design components and sketches:
A) Request classification and routing layer
- Lightweight classifier in front of the load-balancer that tags requests with "latency" or "throughput".
- Inputs: input tokens, estimated output length, customer tier, observed client latency SLO.
- Routing policy table maps "latency" -> prefer nodes with pre-warmed KV-slices + local model shards.
- Implementation note: classifier must be cheap (<1ms) and stateless. Keep it as a request hint rather than a hard constraint.

B) Shard affinity and hot-slice placement
- Maintain a decentralized hot-slice registry: per-model, we track hot kv-key ranges (by hashed prefix) and which GPU owns the primary.
- For latency flows, choose a placement that keeps most hot keys in a single GPU or in NVLink-connected group.
- Eviction policy: occasionally trade off evenness for reduced cross-GPU accesses (heuristic: if top-3 keys cover >40% of recent accesses, collapse them onto one GPU).
- Danger: memory fragmentation and uneven load. Mitigate by time-bounded affinity and background rebalancer.

C) KV coalescing strategy
- Coalesce multiple sequential KV reads from the same prefix into a single prefetch RPC to the owning GPU. Use a small LRU prefetch cache at the serving node.
- For microbatched requests we still do per-request coalesce to avoid interleaving latencies.
- Keep coalescing window tunable (initially 2-3 requests or 10ms) with metrics.

D) NCCL/collective tuning for latency flows
- Use a separate NCCL profile for latency flows: lower chunk size to reduce serialize time; choose ring vs tree based on number of participating GPUs and NIC topology.
- Profile knobs to expose: NCCL_BUFFSIZE, NCCL_NTHREADS, chunk-size, rendezvous threshold.
- Heuristic: prefer ring for small number of GPUs within same NVLink domain; prefer tree (reduce-scatter) for larger cross-host groups to reduce depth.
- Fallback: if NCCL reports overruns or timeouts, automatically raise chunk size or switch algorithm.

E) Kernel pinning and hot-path specialization
- For latency flows, pin commonly-used fused kernels to a low-latency code-path (e.g., fused attention with int8 quantized matmul).
- Maintain a lightweight per-node kernel cache that prioritizes frequently executed kernels for faster JIT warm-up.

F) Scheduler heuristics (microbatch elasticity)
- On latency-tagged requests, avoid enlarging microbatches unless it does not increase p95 (measure via short-window A/B).
- Allow short, opportunistic coalescing for throughput when GPUs are idle but cap at a computed threshold (based on current p95).

Measurements and experiments to run (short-term):
- Experiment A: Route 1% of traffic for a few customers through latency-first path. Measure p50/p95/p99, token cost, and GPU memory spread. Compare against baseline for same customers. (Linked: INF-2379)
- Experiment B: Microbenchmark NCCL ring vs tree vs p2p for 2,4,8 GPU groups on testbed under synthetic NIC noise. Capture latency distribution at varying chunk sizes.
- Experiment C: KV coalescing window sweep (0, 5ms, 10ms, 20ms) measuring additional tail due to coalescing delay vs reduction in cross-GPU RPCs.

Operational considerations and failure modes:
- Memory pressure: affinity may cause OOM on a single GPU. Mitigation: soft caps and immediate fallback to balanced shards; preflight estimator to predict memory use per-affinity decision.
- Hotspotting: too-aggressive collapsing of hot keys can overload single GPUs. Use rate-based backpressure and per-GPU admission controls.
- NCCL stalls: profile and implement circuit-breaker that downgrades chunk-size or switches algorithm mid-request if collectives exceed threshold. This requires careful state management to avoid corrupt KV state but is doable at kernel-level boundaries.

Rollout plan (safe path):
1) Local sim/bench for NCCL profiles and coalescing windows (perf team).
2) Small canary traffic (1–5 customers) with read-only workloads to verify p95 improvements and memory behavior.
3) Gradual expand with feature-flag that allows per-customer opt-in; expose metrics in Console.

Open questions / TODOs:
- How to compute "hot key" ranges deterministically across model versions? (model tokenization differences complicate this).
- What signals to use for classifying latency vs throughput besides token counts (e.g., customer-specified SLOs)?
- Safety net for consistent inference when we move hot-slices across GPUs during an active rollout. Need KV versioning + rollback plan.
- Integration with existing routing layer (PR 812): small refactor may be cleaner than bolting hints onto current LB.

Immediate next steps:
- Miguel: run NCCL microbench (2/4/8 GPUs) and capture per-chunk latency (target: by 2025-09-17).
- Priya: prototype KV coalescing shim in gateway (early PoC by 2025-09-24).
- Connor/Yuna: design safe fallback and admission control sketches (draft by 2025-09-30).
- I will create an experiment dashboard (Console) for p50/p95/p99 and per-GPU memory skew for these canaries.

Notes to self:
- Keep this doc intentionally informal; move formal design into a PR once we have microbench numbers.
- Remember to capture customer opt-in UX and billing implications (latency path could be slightly more expensive).

References and prior art:
- quick notes: attention KV coalescing in other runtimes (internal links), NCCL tuning guide (NVIDIA), REDWOOD-serve past notes on host-offload.

End.
